Our data suggests that visually impaired pedestrians can make accurate and reliable street crossing decisions. However, when using auditory information only, all subjects significantly overestimated the vehicular gap time. This finding indicates that visually impaired pedestrians may benefit from training to improve their detection ability and/or interpretation of vehicular gap times.

On the other hand, blind pedestrians performed significantly worse than either normally sighted or visually impaired subjects under the hearing-only condition. This suggests that they may require additional support or training to accurately navigate street crossings.
